Deploy App is built to be observed: every instance emits structured logs, and the audit log in particular is the authoritative record of who did what to whom. Deploy App defines clear logging and security requirements for its product integrations and for auditability — the goal is that integrations log to the same audit model so activity across the whole stack is recorded consistently (see the status note below). This page describes the audit-log model, what is logged, where logs live, and how logs flow off the host. It is shared across both deployment stacks.

Unified integration logging is still in development. This page describes how the core app (**rmapi**) logs today. Audit logging is not yet unified across the product integrations — right now the core app logs as described here, and integration-API activity must be read from each service's own application logs until then. Carrying full audit context through to the product integration APIs (TAK, Matrix, …) is actively being developed, and this page will be updated as it lands.

The log-shipping and aggregation backend shown below is an example only — substitute your own collector, log store / SIEM, and on-call routing. For certified operators, OpenDefence can share a reference audit-log & alert setup guide with our recommended alert rules, endpoint by endpoint.

Logging objectives

Logging is prioritized around security outcomes, in roughly this order:

Priority Objective Why
Critical Detect unauthorized access attempts mTLS bypass, privilege escalation
Critical Detect container/host compromise Escape attempts, unauthorized CLI access
High Track certificate lifecycle Issuance, revocation, OCSP queries
Medium Audit administrative actions User management, role changes
Medium Monitor service health Availability, performance
Low Operational troubleshooting Debug application issues

Log categories

Logs fall into five categories:

  1. Audit logs — user lifecycle, certificate operations, admin actions.
  2. Security / intrusion logs — privilege escalation, container anomalies, intrusion markers.
  3. Application logs — business logic, errors, stack traces.
  4. Access logs — nginx requests, API calls, mTLS verification results.
  5. System logs — container lifecycle, OS events, resource alerts.

The audit-log model

Audit logging is implemented through python-libpvarki, which adds a dedicated AUDIT log level (Python value 55, mapped to syslog severity 5 / notice). Audit records are emitted as ECS 1.6.0 JSON carried in syslog.

Important scope note: today only rmapi-level (core API) actions are audit-logged. python-libpvarki is planned to be extended later to carry action context through to product integration APIs so that user activity inside products (TAK, etc.) can be audit-logged too. Until then, integration-API activity must be inferred from those services' own application logs.

Audit record fields

Every audit event carries standard ECS 1.6.0 fields plus a few application-specific custom fields:

Field Meaning
event.action Action identifier
event.outcome success, failure, or unknown
user.name Actor performing the action (defaults to the client cert DN if not set explicitly)
destination.user.name Target user of the action
source.ip Original client IP (from X-Real-IP / XFF)
client.ip Direct peer IP (nginx/container)
transaction.id Request correlation ID (X-Request-ID)
tls.client.hash.sha256 Client cert SHA256 fingerprint
tls.client.x509.subject.distinguished_name Client cert DN
tls.client.x509.serial_number Client cert serial
error_message / error_code Detail and reason code for failures
invitecode_id Invite code UUID (never the raw code value)
certificate_type pem or pfx

Log formats and levels

The core rmapi service controls the log format via the LOG_CONSOLE_FORMATTER environment variable:

LOG_CONSOLE_FORMATTER=local    # human-readable (development/local)
LOG_CONSOLE_FORMATTER=ecs      # ECS JSON (legacy, being phased out)
LOG_CONSOLE_FORMATTER=syslog   # ECS JSON-in-syslog (target for rm* services)

OpenDefence rm* services (including takrmapi) are migrating from plain ECS JSON to ECS-JSON-in-syslog. Third-party components (Keycloak, MediaMTX, CFSSL) keep their native formats. The core rmapi emits its logs and audit logs in ECS-JSON-in-syslog.

Per-component log levels:

Component Framework Level env var Prod default
rmapi libpvarki.logging RM_LOG_LEVEL INFO
keycloak Quarkus/Java KC_LOG_LEVEL INFO
nginx native error_log directive WARN
ocsprest libadvian.logging -l / --loglevel 30 (WARNING)
takrmapi libpvarki.logging LOG_LEVEL INFO
postgres native log_min_messages WARNING
openldap slapd LDAP_LOGLEVEL 0
cfssl native --loglevel 1 (INFO)

Syslog severity mapping for the Python services (priority shown for the local0 facility):

Python level Value Syslog severity Priority
AUDIT 55 5 (notice) 133
CRITICAL 50 2 (critical) 130
ERROR 40 3 (error) 131
WARNING 30 4 (warning) 132
INFO 20 6 (info) 134
DEBUG 10 7 (debug) 135

Logging architecture

The diagram traces a log line from the Deploy App host to your on-call. The aggregation tier is an example — substitute your own log-shipping agent, central log store / SIEM, and alert routing.

        Agent["Log-shipping agent"]

    end

On the legacy Docker Compose stack the syslog log driver is configured in Docker, and a log store ingests the syslog stream (the ECS JSON inside it stays queryable). On Kubernetes the platform ships its own monitoring stack (Loki / Grafana / Alloy / Prometheus, deployed as the monitoring phase) — see Deploy on Kubernetes.

Where logs live

Log type Location Access method
All container stdout/stderr /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/*.log docker compose logs
nginx access stdout (Docker-captured) docker compose logs rmnginx
TAK server /opt/tak/logs/ in tak_data volume docker exec into the container
PostgreSQL pg_data volume docker compose logs postgres
CFSSL/OCSP stdout + /data/persistent/ container logs + volume

Retention on a local instance is the instance lifetime (no automatic rotation by default); the recommended Docker daemon config is max-size: 100m, max-file: 5. Centralized retention is whatever your log store's policy sets.

Accessing logs

Direct (SSH / emergency / dev):

# Real-time, all services
docker compose logs -f

# Specific services with timestamps
docker compose logs -f --timestamps rmapi keycloak rmnginx cfssl ocsprest

# Export the last 24h for analysis
docker compose logs --since 24h --no-color > /tmp/logs-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).log

Centralized (primary in test/prod-like environments): query the aggregated stream from your log store / SIEM. Set access policy per environment — for example route normal access through the log store and reserve SSH for emergencies.

Health checks

Quick per-service health endpoints (legacy ports):

curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/v1/healthcheck     # rmapi
curl -s http://keycloak:8080/health/ready | grep -q UP  # keycloak
curl -s http://localhost:8887/api/v1/healthcheck     # ocsprest (returns crlfail if CRL stale)
curl -s http://localhost:5666/healthcheck            # nginx internal
curl -s http://localhost:8003/api/v1/healthcheck     # takrmapi
Organization-wide logging and documentation conventions are deferred to the Community & Standards page (in Contribute to Project).
